query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding trace amounts of reactive elements (e.g., Y and Hf) during alloy production will enhance the grain‐boundary stability and oxide scale adherence of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy, thereby improving its resistance to high-temperature creep and corrosion without compromising its inherent strength–ductility balance.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a fine, uniform lamellar (fcc/B2) structure.
generation.intervention: Introduce minor dopants (on the order of 0.5–1 atomic percent each of Y and Hf) into the alloy during melting and casting.
generation.conditions: Performance evaluated under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading (creep at room temperature and elevated temperatures), and corrosive environments (e.g., salt-laden atmospheres typical of aerospace/spacecraft fasteners).
generation.structural_mediator: Dopant segregation at grain boundaries and phase interfaces that leads to a more coherent and adherent oxide layer and suppressed diffusion paths.
generation.mechanism: Reactive elements preferentially segregate to grain boundaries and phase interfaces. This segregation reduces grain-boundary diffusion (thereby mitigating creep) and promotes the formation of a stable, adherent oxide scale that resists spallation during thermal cycling and corrosive attack.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, the doped alloy is expected to exhibit lower room-temperature creep strain rates, longer creep lifetimes, and reduced corrosion (e.g., lower spallation and mass loss), all while maintaining a strength–ductility balance similar to or slightly improved over the undoped alloy.
generation.baseline: The as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy currently showing good strength and ductility but limited long-term creep and corrosion resistance for aerospace/space fastener applications.
generation.boundary: The benefits are anticipated only when dopant levels are kept low enough to avoid phase segregation or embrittlement, and when processing conditions remain similar to conventional casting methods.
generation.uncertainty: The optimum dopant concentration and processing parameters that maximize creep and corrosion improvements without affecting mechanical performance are yet to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: a control group using the standard AlCoCrFeNi2.1 composition and an experimental group with 0.5–1 at% each of Y and Hf added. Process both series via conventional casting to obtain similar fine lamellar microstructures. Subject the samples to cyclic thermal fluctuation tests and long-term creep loading under controlled laboratory conditions, as well as electrochemical corrosion tests simulating a salt-containing environment.
measurements: Creep strain rate and creep rupture life under sustained load at both room and elevated temperatures
Corrosion rate (mass loss measurements and/or electrochemical corrosion potential monitoring)
Tensile strength and ductility from mechanical testing before and after environmental exposures
Microstructural analysis (grain boundary segregation of dopants, oxide scale integrity, and phase stability)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the doped alloy does not exhibit statistically significant improvements in creep resistance and corrosion performance (while maintaining comparable strength and ductility) relative to the control samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractBoth crack-free AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) and Y and Hf co-doping AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA (YHf-EHEA) coatings were prepared by laser cladding. The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. The experimental results showed that the structure of the as-deposited coatings consisted of FCC and BCC/B2 phases. After heat treatment, an Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC phase of all coatings. The grain sizes of the EHEA and YHf-EHEA coatings after heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h increased by 27.5% and 15.7%, respectively, compared to the as-deposited coatings. Meanwhile, after hot corrosion, the spallation areas of the YHf-EHEA and EHEA coatings accounted for 14.98% and 5.67% of the total surface area, respectively. As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications.
